## What this question is asking

Question 4 asks us to do one of two things, compared to the in-class model:

-   find a **simpler** panel (fewer proteins) that works about as well, or
-   find a **better** panel (any method) that works even more accurately

We tried both, then double-checked everything with a fairer testing method
at the end. Full working code is in `scripts/varun/question4.R`.

## Metric definitions (in plain words)

-   **Sensitivity:** out of the kids who actually have ASD, how many did
    we correctly catch?
-   **Specificity:** out of the kids who don't have ASD, how many did we
    correctly clear?
-   **Accuracy:** out of all kids, how many did we get right overall?
-   **AUROC:** how good the model is at ranking "more likely ASD" above
    "less likely ASD" (0.5 = random guessing, 1 = perfect)

## Starting point: the in-class benchmark

The in-class model used **5 proteins** (DERM, RELT, MRC2, IgD,
Cadherin-5), picked by taking the top 10 proteins from a statistical test
and the top 10 from a random forest, then keeping only the ones that
showed up on *both* lists.

**Benchmark results:** sensitivity 0.812, specificity 0.733, accuracy
0.774, AUROC 0.883.

One thing we noticed looking closer at this model: when we checked which
of the 5 proteins were actually statistically meaningful on their own,
only **2 of them** were -- DERM and IgD. The other 3 (RELT, MRC2,
Cadherin-5) weren't pulling real weight. That became our starting idea
for a simpler panel.

## Try 1: A simpler panel (just DERM + IgD)

**Setup:** same data, same training/test split as the benchmark -- we
only changed which proteins go into the model, dropping from 5 down to
just the 2 that mattered.

**Results (same 31 test kids as the benchmark):**

| Metric      | Benchmark (5 proteins) | Simple panel (2 proteins) |
|-------------|------------------------|----------------------------|
| Sensitivity | 0.812                  | 0.812                      |
| Specificity | 0.733                  | 0.733                      |
| Accuracy    | 0.774                  | 0.774                      |
| AUROC       | 0.883                  | 0.850                      |

**Interpretation:** three of the four scores are *exactly* the same, and
the fourth (AUROC) only dropped a little. So cutting the panel from 5
proteins down to 2 barely changed anything.

**Takeaway:** DERM and IgD alone do almost all the work. The other 3
proteins weren't adding much.

**Caveat:** this test only used one small group of 31 kids, so small
differences could just be luck, not a real difference. (We fix this
further down.)

## Try 2: Let a smarter method pick the panel automatically (LASSO)

**Setup:** instead of picking proteins with a statistical test + random
forest like the in-class method, we used a method called **LASSO**. It
looks at *all* 1,317 proteins at once and automatically decides which
ones matter and which ones to ignore -- no need to pre-filter by hand.

**Results (same 31 test kids):**

| Metric      | Benchmark (5) | LASSO, looser (46 proteins) | LASSO, stricter (17 proteins) |
|-------------|---------------|------------------------------|--------------------------------|
| Sensitivity | 0.812         | 0.562                        | 0.625                          |
| Specificity | 0.733         | 0.933                        | 0.867                          |
| Accuracy    | 0.774         | 0.742                        | 0.742                          |
| AUROC       | 0.883         | 0.913                        | 0.908                          |

**Interpretation:** LASSO is better at ranking who's more likely to have
ASD (higher AUROC) and much better at avoiding false alarms (higher
specificity) -- but it's noticeably worse at actually catching true ASD
cases (lower sensitivity), and its accuracy is a bit lower too. It also
needs way more proteins, so it's not "simpler" either.

**Takeaway:** LASSO is a trade-off, not a clear win. Good at one thing
(ranking/avoiding false alarms), worse at another (catching real cases).

**Side note:** LASSO independently backs up our earlier finding --
MRC2 and Cadherin-5 never got picked by LASSO at all, and RELT only
showed up in the loosest version. A totally different method agrees
those proteins aren't very useful.

**Caveat:** same as before -- based on one 31-kid test group, so numbers
could be noisy.

## Making it fair: testing everything properly

**The problem:** every result above came from testing on the *same* 31
kids, one time. With so few kids, getting even 1 extra kid right or wrong
changes "accuracy" by about 3 percentage points. So small differences
between panels might just be random luck, not a real difference.

**The fix:** instead of testing once, we used **repeated cross-validation**
-- split the 154 kids into 10 groups, test on each group once while
training on the rest, then repeat that whole process 10 times with
different groupings. Every kid ends up being tested on about 10 times, so
the final numbers are an average, not a one-time guess.

**Results (fair, averaged comparison):**

| Panel                      | # proteins | Accuracy | AUROC | Sensitivity | Specificity |
|-----------------------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **DERM + IgD (simple)**     | **2** | **0.744** | 0.801 | **0.775** | 0.715 |
| DERM + IgD + RELT           | 3   | 0.735 | **0.814** | 0.747 | 0.728 |
| Original benchmark          | 5   | 0.730 | 0.791 | 0.741 | 0.724 |
| Combined list (both methods)| 15  | 0.713 | 0.795 | 0.700 | 0.727 |
| LASSO (auto-picked)         | ~17-46 | 0.708 | 0.819 | 0.667 | **0.778** |

**Interpretation:**

-   The simple **2-protein panel comes out on top** for accuracy and
    sensitivity -- not just "as good as" the original, actually a little
    *better*, once tested fairly.
-   **More proteins made things worse, not better.** The 15-protein and
    LASSO versions scored lower on accuracy than the simple 2-protein
    panel. This is called **overfitting** -- with so few kids to learn
    from, using too many proteins lets the model latch onto noise instead
    of real patterns, so it does worse on new kids even though it looks
    more sophisticated on paper.
-   LASSO's trade-off (better ranking/specificity, worse at catching real
    cases) held up even under this fairer test -- so that finding is
    solid, not just a fluke.

**Takeaway / final answer for Question 4:** the **2-protein DERM + IgD
panel** is our recommended result. It is simpler than the original
(2 proteins instead of 5) **and** performs slightly better on accuracy
and sensitivity once tested fairly -- so it satisfies both goals of this
question at the same time.

**Caveats (overall limitations):**

-   The whole dataset is only 154 kids, which is small for this kind of
    model -- even with fair testing, the numbers can shift a bit with
    different random splits.
-   None of this tells us *why* DERM and IgD matter biologically --
    that would need outside medical/scientific knowledge, not just data.
-   These results describe this one dataset; they may not generalize to
    a different group of kids without being tested again.
